items.title: Agentic Influence Operations: A Multi-Dimensional Governance Framework for Generative AI-Enabled Information Disorder in Multimedia Ecosystems
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), synthetic media, social bots, and agentic AI are turning information disorder from a content-verification problem into a governance problem for multimedia information ecosystems. Research on fake news, deepfakes, GenAI misuse, and cyber-enabled influence has developed in largely separate streams, and none of these streams offers an integrated governance model for influence activity coordinated through AI-supported workflows. This study develops such a model through a structured evidence synthesis of 35 peer-reviewed sources published between 2019 and 2026, identified through four structured discovery queries and citation chaining and appraised with evidence-type-specific criteria. The synthesis identifies five mechanisms through which AI reshapes information disorder: influence orchestration, ambiguity production, selective persuasion, hybrid human–machine dissemination, and a trust paradox in countermeasures. On this basis, the study defines agentic influence operations as workflow-level risks and organizes them in a twelve-dimension framework that links AI capabilities, content modality, platform infrastructure, data access, evidentiary trust, organizational harm, and governance control points. It also sets out construct boundary conditions, five propositions with explicit evidence status, a managerial control set, and a phased implementation roadmap. Only the proposition on synthetic media and uncertainty about authentic evidence has direct empirical support; the others are offered for testing through simulation, experimental, design-science, and expert-validation studies.

items.title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents accomplish complex tasks through multi-turn interactions with external tools. However, malicious content embedded in user queries, tool descriptions, or environment observations can manipulate their decisions and induce unsafe actions. Adversarial co-evolution has emerged as an effective approach to strengthening LLM safety, but existing work primarily focuses on language-level safety or indirect prompt injection in web tasks. In this paper, we introduce AgentSafeEvo, a co-evolutionary reinforcement learning framework for agent safety built on an attacker-defender game spanning diverse tasks and attack types. The attacker learns to construct adversarial agent tasks that expose weaknesses in the defender's tool use, while the defender learns to complete tasks safely under these attacks. We further introduce learnability-guided task weighting, which uses within-task defender-reward variability to adjust each task's contribution to attacker and defender updates. Extensive experiments on agent safety and general capability benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves adversarial robustness while maintaining general agent capabilities.

items.title: AI Agents and Agentic AI: What Sets Them Apart?
items.abstract: The distinction between AI agents and agentic AI is conceptually defensible when it separates an entitythat acts, the properties of its behavior, and the system that enables goal completion. However, theliterature and providers do not establish a universal boundary between two technologies. An agent cancarry out extended processes, and an agentic system can contain a single agent. This article examinesacademic antecedents, contrasts recent taxonomies, and compares terminology used by OpenAI,Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and other providers. It offers an explicitly non-consensus teachingframework and explains why autonomy, agent count, content generation, learning, and authority shouldbe analyzed separately. Keywords: AI; intelligent agents; agentic AI; autonomy; multi-agent systems; language models;governance.

items.title: AI Agents in Decentralised Social Networks: A Quasi-Experimental Field Study on Behavioural and Structural Dynamics in Farcaster
items.abstract: Why can similarly configured AI agents amplify engagement in some communities yet mainly redirect it in others? We deployed two autonomous AI agents in separate Farcaster channels (January–February 2026) across two incentive phases: Phase 1 with $Degen token rewards and Phase 2 with social recognition through agent follow-backs and mutual-follow encouragement. In /replyors (71 daily replies at baseline, Attention Saturation Ratio 1.17), the difference-in-differences (DiD)-adjusted engagement lift was +228% in Phase 1 and +118% in Phase 2, consistent with engagement amplification, although the seven-day baseline does not establish parallel pre-treatment trends cleanly. In /degen (244 daily replies, ASR 2.17), the channel-level DiD estimate was +18% (p = 0.71) and not statistically distinguishable from zero despite strong topic-level participation. Because the available /degen–/base control is poorly matched on baseline scale and ASR, that comparison is treated as suggestive rather than a clean causal estimate. Phase 1 generated 967 participant reply messages from 61 unique individuals and 101,980 $Degen distributed. Using historical DEGEN/USD closes at the beginning and end of the 9–22 January reward phase as a broad valuation bracket, the aggregate token budget was on the order of US$111–152; this is not a transaction-time weighted valuation. After token removal, participant reply volume within agent-initiated threads fell by approximately 82–90% and Phase 1 participant retention was 27–34%. We introduce the Contextual Amplification Framework (CAF) and Attention Saturation Ratio (ASR) as provisional, exploratory constructs derived from two treated channels. The evidence is consistent with the possibility that pre-existing attention saturation moderates agent effects, but the ASR is not a validated screening rule and requires multi-site replication. The findings carry implications for platform economics, AI governance, and token incentive design.

items.title: AI and I—Distributed Authorships in the Swedish Upper Secondary Writing Classroom
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines upper secondary students’ writing with Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) through a post-structural lens. The aim is to explore how authorship can be understood and described in the age of AI. The empirical material consists of three students’ recorded writing sessions and complementary interviews. Through rhizomatic mapping, the recordings are analyzed with Deleuze and Guattari’s notions of assemblage, affect and becoming, further extended through the concept of distributed authorship. The analyses map three dynamic assemblages in which writing and authorship are redistributed across heterogeneous relations. One assemblage foregrounds AI as the primary authorial agent; another enacts reciprocal human-AI co-writing; and a third positions AI as a threat to writing, creativity, and the climate. Writing with GenAI unfolds as a complex relational practice and authorship emerges as distributed between humans and non-humans. This study raises important questions for education to consider in writing instruction and in developing policies for writing with AI, such as questions of equity and ethics.

items.title: AI Co‐Host Adoption and Traffic Governance in Live Commerce: Human Effort Incentives and Architecture Switching
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) virtual streamers are making live‐commerce selling increasingly scalable, yet human explanation and trust remain central to purchase conversion. This paper develops a Stackelberg model of AI co‐host adoption under algorithmic traffic bias. The platform first chooses a transaction commission and an AI‐oriented traffic bias, after which the brand selects AI‐only selling, human‐only selling, or AI‐human co‐host selling. When a human streamer participates, the brand offers a performance commission, and the streamer chooses costly explanation effort. Algorithmic traffic allocation shapes both market exposure and the marginal return to human effort. Greater AI‐oriented traffic bias weakens effort under human‐only selling but strengthens it under AI‐human co‐hosting by enlarging the revenue base for human explanation. Once AI traffic support makes AI‐only selling more profitable than co‐hosting, human effort drops discontinuously to zero. The model identifies when AI co‐hosting complements human streamers, when traffic support instead induces substitution, and why a commission‐driven platform may favor more AI‐oriented exposure than a welfare‐aware benchmark. Extensions with return risk and two‐part contracts clarify how product fit and compensation design affect the value of co‐hosting. Robustness analyses show that the main qualitative results continue to hold under bounded nonlinear traffic allocation, nonlinear demand, and binding contract constraints.

items.title: AI dependency and employee burnout: a nonlinear self-determination perspective
items.abstract: Purpose Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study aims to examine how employees’ artificial intelligence (AI) dependency is associated with burnout in hospitality. It tests the curvilinear nature of this association, the roles of competence and autonomy as need-related pathways and the moderating role of perceived organizational support (POS). Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 375 AI-using hospitality employees in China through a three-wave time-lagged survey. The measurement model was validated using confirmatory factor analysis. Hypotheses were tested using hierarchical regression with quadratic and interaction terms, and conditional indirect effects were examined using a derivative-based approach with delta-method confidence intervals. Findings AI dependency was associated with burnout in a U-shaped pattern with burnout decreasing from low to moderate dependency and increasing at higher dependency. Consistent with SDT AI dependency was associated with competence and autonomy in inverted U-shaped patterns. Competence and autonomy helped account for this curvilinear association with moderate dependency linked to higher competence and autonomy and lower burnout and high dependency linked to the opposite pattern. POS attenuated the negative curvature in these relationships fundamentally altering how AI dependency relates to employees psychological needs at higher AI dependency levels. Research limitations/implications This study extends hospitality technology and employee well-being research by conceptualizing AI dependency as a nonlinear antecedent of burnout and by integrating SDT with POS as a boundary condition. It clarifies when AI-enabled work shifts from supporting psychological needs to undermining them, and offers a mechanism-based explanation of how organizations can preserve employee well-being as AI becomes embedded in hospitality workflows. Originality/value This study advances hospitality AI and employee well-being research by shifting attention from AI use and adoption to employees’ perceived AI dependency. It develops a nonlinear SDT-based framework that explains how AI dependency is linked to burnout through competence and autonomy and identifies POS as a contextual boundary condition in AI-enabled hospitality work.

items.title: AI in education: boosting productivity or challenging cognitive effort?
items.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education by changing how students learn and perform academic tasks. Although AI is associated with greater time efficiency and improved academic performance, its broader effects on student productivity and cognitive effort remain insufficiently understood. This study aims to examine how university students associate AI-led productivity gains with less study time, better grades, better understanding of study material, changes in cognitive effort they put into AI-supported task completion and dependency on AI tools. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted an exploratory survey among university students in Hanoi in late 2024 and proposed an empirical model that pools self-reported time efficiency, academic performance, academic self-efficacy, change in cognitive effort and AI dependency as dimensions of student productivity. The authors control for AI use intensity and AI use in collaboration, as well as for some other socio-demographic characteristics. Given the exploratory nature of the study and the relatively small sample, the empirical analysis follows a staged specification strategy when the authors first estimate a parsimonious baseline model and subsequently introduce two sets of background controls sequentially. The authors further estimate an interaction between cognitive effort change and AI dependency, first in a parsimonious specification and subsequently with additional controls. Finally, the authors produce a sensitivity analysis of the model to alternative operationalisation of self-efficacy variable. Findings Students associate their AI-led productivity gains primarily with less study time, a bit less so with better grades and better understanding of the study material. They also associate the productivity growth with greater changes of cognitive effort they put into problem-solving while using AI and rising dependency on AI tools. Self-confidence appears to be associated with likelihood to reap significant rather than some productivity gains particularly once the interaction of AI dependency and AI-led cognitive shift is accounted for. The survey data also support the existence of potentially uneven academic benefits from AI use when higher-achieving students are more likely to report further improvements in academic performance, whereas students with weaker prior performance report rather limited gains. Research limitations/implications The findings highlight the need for research design that captures the dynamic evolution of AI-supported learning. The observed differences between daily and weekly users, particularly in critical evaluation and perceived accuracy, suggest that future studies should examine how evaluative skills and cognitive effort develop over time. Longitudinal and experimental designs, combined with objective performance and AI-usage data, would allow researchers to test whether the productivity dimensions proposed here operate causally or how much the fast-paced evolution of AI tools changes the cognitive effort students put into problem-solving and critical thinking when completing academic tasks, and their dependency on AI tools for academic productivity. Practical implications The results provide actionable guidance for universities seeking to integrate AI into teaching and assessment practices. The strong role of time efficiency and self-efficacy, alongside uneven benefits across student groups, indicates the need for structured AI literacy modules that teach source verification and evaluative strategies and effective prompt formulation. Given that daily users show higher critical evaluation but lower perceived accuracy, teaching practices should incorporate reflective assignments that require students to justify, critique and revise AI-generated content. Assessment formats may need redesign to ensure transparent AI use while still requiring independent reasoning, analytical justification and domain-specific understanding. Social implications Policies should balance the productivity benefits of AI-supported learning with safeguards that promote independent thinking, academic integrity and equitable access. Addressing disparities in AI literacy and access is essential to prevent the widening of the existing academic inequalities. Originality/value This study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-assisted learning by examining students’ perceived productivity gains alongside several concurrent dimensions of their AI-supported academic experience, including time efficiency, perceived academic performance, academic self-efficacy, changes in cognitive effort and AI dependency. Rather than proposing these dimensions as new constructs or causal mechanisms, this study brings them together within a single analytical framework. Particular attention is given to whether perceived productivity gains and growing reliance on AI coexist with self-reported changes in cognitive effort, an interplay that remains insufficiently explored in the existing research. Empirically, this study provides exploratory evidence from Vietnam, an underrepresented higher education context in Southeast Asia.

items.title: AI literacy and STEM education: emerging frontiers and research priorities
items.abstract: Abstract This article examines the state of the art in AI literacy and STEM education and identifies emerging frontiers and research priorities to inspire cutting-edge empirical and theoretical research. The reviewed research is grounded in established AI literacy frameworks and shows that there is potential for students’ development of a critical and technologically informed AI literacy. However, the research is unevenly spread across the STEM disciplines and the potential for AI to transform STEM learning remains unclear. Thus, while the field has expanded rapidly, particularly with the emergence of generative AI (GenAI), fundamental challenges remain. The conceptual ambiguity surrounding AI literacy, combined with the rapid evolution of AI technologies, demands continued theoretical refinement and empirical investigation. Critical questions remain regarding how AI literacy intersects with disciplinary STEM literacies, how GenAI tools both support and reshape teaching and learning processes, and what opportunities and trade-offs arise when students engage with AI as learning partner. The ethical dilemmas of AI integration, including bias, data privacy, and environmental sustainability, also warrant urgent attention. As STEM education increasingly engages with AI as both a subject of learning and a learning tool, future research must move beyond one-size-fits-all frameworks toward context-sensitive approaches that empower educators and learners to critically and responsibly engage with AI while preserving core STEM learning goals. items.title: AI Revolution and Scientific Research Involving LLMs and Gen-AI: Preliminary PICO-AI, SPIDER-AI, and PRISMA-AI Conceptual Extensions for Evidence Synthesis Frameworks
items.abstract: Background: Systematic and scoping reviews rely on established frameworks such as PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome), SPIDER (Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation, Research type), and PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) to structure research questions, guide evidence synthesis, and ensure transparent reporting. These frameworks were developed for linear, human-driven workflows involving manual searching, screening, and data extraction. The emergence of large language models (LLMs) and Generative AI (Gen-AI) introduces new capabilities for semi-automated literature discovery, screening, data extraction, and thematic synthesis. However, the methodological implications of AI-assisted evidence synthesis remain underexplored. Methods: This manuscript employed a scoping review–informed methodological analysis of empirical and methodological literature located through structured searches of PubMed and Google Scholar. Preliminary conceptual extensions to PICO, SPIDER, and PRISMA were developed, retrospectively applied to published studies, and independently evaluated by five researchers for applicability, relevance, and clarity. Results: LLMs enable dynamic and iterative processes across evidence synthesis stages, including automated question formulation, large-scale qualitative analysis, and hybrid human–AI screening and extraction. These developments challenge the linear assumptions of PICO, SPIDER, and PRISMA. In response, PICO-AI, SPIDER-AI, and PRISMA-AI incorporate dimensions including prompt transparency, model specification, human-in-the-loop validation, Human–AI workflow classification, data governance, and AI auditability. Independent evaluation showed 80% item agreement, with overall mean relevance and clarity ratings of 3.2/4. Conclusions: LLMs and Gen-AI do not replace systematic review frameworks; rather, they extend them by introducing adaptive, data-driven workflows. Integrating AI into evidence synthesis requires revised methodological guidance to ensure transparency, reproducibility, and rigour. The proposed preliminary extensions provide a model for incorporating machine intelligence into systematic and scoping review practices.

items.title: AI Swarm Intelligence Must Be Studied as a Sociotechnical Phenomenon
items.abstract: The emergence of coordinated autonomous AI agents is fundamentally altering human belief systems and public discourse at scales and speeds that outpace existing characterization methods. This paper argues that AI swarm intelligence, the coordinated influence of autonomous agents on human populations, represents a phase shift that cannot be understood by simply scaling single-agent analysis. Instead, it must be analyzed as a sociotechnical system where societal impact emerges from the tight coupling of individual agent capabilities, multi-agent coordination, and population dynamics. Because the shift from single- to multi-agent systems corresponds to a psychological transition between single- and multiple-source influence, we propose a unified framework and evaluate these systems across operational, individual, and population-level dynamics. We identify concrete research agendas and call on the community to build the evaluation methods, countermeasures, and governance approaches needed to address the long-term societal impact of these coordinated autonomous AI populations. items.title: AI use and risk disclosure by investment advisers
items.abstract: Introduction Investment advisers increasingly report using artificial intelligence (AI), but little is known about what they disclose about it in fiduciary filings. The SEC brought its first AI-washing enforcement actions in 2024, so regulators and researchers need a reproducible measure of AI disclosure. We provide large-sample evidence on AI disclosure in Form ADV Part 2A brochures and show how the estimate depends on measurement design. Methods We drew a stratified random sample of 400 SEC-registered investment advisers from a population of 16,223 firms, crossing adviser type (private-fund vs. wealth/retail) with 2024 assets-under-management (AUM) quartile. A large language model (LLM) classified the 388 available brochures under a prespecified five-label typology: investment-process use, operational or client-service use, AI-related risk, explicit non-use, and named AI vendors. We treated the LLM as a measurement instrument and validated it three ways: same-family reproducibility, blinded cross-family recoding of 180 brochures, and human verification of 158 cases. Secondary analyses compared brochures with 283 matched firm websites and applied a screen derived from SEC enforcement orders. Results AI use is disclosed in 23.7% of brochures (22.7% survey-weighted), while 27.6% contain AI-related risk language. The within-brochure difference is significant (McNemar p = 0.036). Disclosure rises from 10.4% in the smallest AUM quartile to 43.8% in the largest, and is higher among private-fund advisers. Against human coding, the composite any-use measure achieves precision of 0.76 and sensitivity of 0.81. The same corpus yields estimates of 9.9%, 13.1%, and 23.7% under alternative constructs, adviser universes, and weighting schemes. A literal keyword rule misses or mislabels roughly a quarter of cases. A raw 17.3-percentage-point brochure–website gap disappears after conditioning on document length. None of the five enforcement-screen matches was adjudicated as an unsubstantiated promotional claim. Discussion Advisers present AI at least as often as a risk as a capability, and disclosure is concentrated among larger and private-fund advisers. AI-disclosure prevalence reflects measurement design as much as adviser behavior, so estimates should be reported with their construct, universe, weighting, and validation. The validated framework and an open reproducibility capsule provide a baseline for monitoring AI claims and AI-washing in investment management.

items.title: AI virtual assistance in recruitment: a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis
items.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into recruitment, focusing on the underexplored role of AI virtual assistants (AIVA). This study aims to evaluate how AIVA transforms recruitment practices and to provide a systematic research agenda for future applications. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted a systematic literature review (SLR) and a bibliometric analysis (BA) to assess the use of AIVA in recruitment over the past decade, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines. A structured search of the Scopus and Web of Science databases identified 5,301 publications from 2015 to June 1, 2026. After screening, the authors selected 255 papers for full-text review and BA, using R and VOSviewer. They systematically summarized and guided the exploration of current research. Findings The findings suggest that AIVA affects every phase of the recruitment process, from identifying staffing requirements to onboarding new personnel, with publications increasing significantly after 2023. The thematic analysis identified four key themes: isolated mature areas, innovation drivers, transitional uncertainties and broad foundational concepts. In addition, this SLR and BA critically examined the existing literature, highlighting advances and identifying gaps for future research. It also proposed a research agenda to guide subsequent investigations. Research limitations/implications This study is limited to publications indexed in Scopus and Web of Science, which potentially excludes relevant literature. Future research should expand to diverse data sets and explore the longitudinal impacts of AIVA adoption. Practical implications The findings provide actionable pathways for Human Resources (HR) practitioners to integrate AIVA into recruitment, thereby improving decision-making and reducing inefficiencies. Social implications AIVA adoption may improve recruitment equity, fairness, inclusivity and efficiency. Originality/value This paper uniquely synthesizes recruitment literature on AIVA through a dual SLR and BA approach. It advances theory by operationalizing broad AI research directions into domain-specific insights and offers practical implications for reducing recruitment costs, enhancing efficiency and guiding stakeholders in adopting AIVA.

items.title: AI-assisted characterization of psychedelic clinical trials from ClinicalTrials.gov
items.abstract: Abstract Background The registry record of psychedelic and related rapid-acting compounds is large, heterogeneous and laborious to synthesize by hand. We tested whether a large language model (LLM) with live access to the ClinicalTrials.gov application programming interface (API) could produce a timely, structured and reproducible characterization of this landscape. Methods Cross-sectional analysis of interventional trials on ClinicalTrials.gov as of 13 January 2026. The core-set comprised classic serotonin 5-HT2A agonists, MDMA, ibogaine and ayahuasca; ketamine and esketamine in psychiatric indications formed a separately reported comparator class. Claude (Anthropic), connected to the registry API, retrieved records first through open-ended natural-language querying and then through a documented protocol of field-specific query expressions restricted to records first posted by the search date, which yielded every reported count; populations and indications were defined from structured registry fields. Results Excluding withdrawn records, 412 core-set trials were identified (256 in patients), plus 300 ketamine/esketamine trials. Psilocybin accounted for 244 (59%; 181 in patients), MDMA 99 (47), LSD 39 (13), DMT/5-MeO-DMT 36 (12), ayahuasca 6 and ibogaine 4. Depression led for psilocybin (74 of 181 patient trials) and the ketamine class (237 of 300), PTSD for MDMA (35 of 47) and anxiety for LSD (6 of 13). Of 63 phase 2/3 psilocybin trials in depression, 35 (56%) had a depression rating scale as primary endpoint, most often the MADRS (25), 34 (54%) assessed it at weeks 3–6, 26 (41%) excluded adults over 65 and none enrolled adolescents. Twenty-four core-set trials were registered as phase 3, 13 of psilocybin; psilocybin phase 3 programmes plan more than 1900 participants, the pivotal MDMA trials enrolled 100 and 121, LSD phase 3 trials plan 149–245, and no other psychedelic had a phase 3 trial. Five patient trials (2%) had a site in a low- or middle-income country. Conclusions LLM-mediated registry querying yielded a structured, reproducible characterization of a fast-moving field, but only once each count was tied to an explicit, archived query expression; open-ended conversational querying had underestimated the record several-fold for some compounds. The approach complements rather than replaces systematic review, and its accuracy against manual extraction remains to be quantified.

items.title: AI-Assisted WES Variant Interpretation in Neurodevelopmental Disorders: A Narrative Review of Existing Tools
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of conditions characterized by alterations in brain development and function, frequently associated with complex genetic architectures. The widespread implementation of next-generation sequencing, particularly whole-exome sequencing (WES), has substantially increased the identification of potentially disease-associated variants, shifting the major challenge from variant detection to their interpretation and prioritization. This review examines the emerging contribution of artificial intelligence (AI) to WES variant interpretation in NDDs, with particular emphasis on AI-assisted variant prioritization and protein structural modelling. Methods: We reviewed conventional computational and emerging AI-driven approaches applicable to different stages of WES interpretation, including variant pathogenicity and functional-effect prediction, evolutionary conservation, splicing assessment, phenotype-informed prioritization, and protein structure prediction. Their methodological principles, applications, and major limitations were critically examined within the context of neurodevelopmental genomics. Results: AI and machine-learning approaches increasingly integrate genomic, phenotypic, functional, and structural information, supporting phenotype-aware candidate prioritization and molecular contextualization of selected variants. However, computational outputs are affected by model-specific limitations and should not be considered independent evidence of pathogenicity. Their added value depends primarily on the complementarity and biological relevance of the information provided, rather than on predictor concordance alone. Conclusions: This narrative review highlights that AI-assisted WES interpretation should prioritize complementary, mechanism-relevant evidence over computational concordance. AI-assisted tools should therefore be selected according to variant class and disease mechanism and integrated with independent clinical, genetic, and functional evidence.

items.title: AI-Based Intent Normalization and Service Routing in Distributed Agentic Microservices
items.abstract: LLMs are increasingly being embedded into a variety of distributed agentic systems, in the form of agents with APIs, microservices, workflows, and external tools for task completion. Systems need to be able to handle requests that are worded differently but mean the same thing, to make sure routing is consistent, caching can be reused, latency is reduced, reliability is ensured, and governance is supported. Conventional intent representations, beyond simply conveying what users want with their intent and respective slots, do not encode information about user authorization, policies with implications for execution, side effects of actions, locality of execution, and operational implications of intents. Prior work has provided frameworks for normalization, capability discovery and routing in distributed agentic systems, but all this work is done independently and thus does not provide a unified pipeline for handling requests in distributed systems. The main contribution of this paper is to propose a unified framework describing the normalization, discovery, routing, execution control and runtime feedback in distributed agentic systems. The core of this work is the introduction of a canonical representation of intent, called an intent record, which can convey all kinds of semantic information, as well as context, policy, and operational information about the system as a whole, including its uncertainty, to be used by the system’s routing layer. We also introduce a new constraint-first multi-criteria routing process. A reference architecture is also given for such sorts of systems. The architecture’s main functional components are semantic control and its decoupled, cross-governance-deterministic execution. An evaluation framework for the proposed approach in the future is also presented. This framework is not validated through implementation or benchmarking experiments. Such an empirical evaluation is left for future work.

items.title: AI-based relighting in moving images: current potentials, limitations, and implications for cinematographic practice
items.abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) continuously opens up new possibilities in film post-production, including the subsequent relighting of moving images. As a systematic assessment from a film-design and professional-practice perspective has been lacking, this study examines the potentials, limitations, and implications of current AI-based relighting workflows for cinematographic practice. Methodologically, the study follows a qualitative-exploratory research design within practice-based and practice-led frameworks. Three current AI-based relighting systems (Nvidia DiffusionRenderer, Beeble Studio, and SwitchX) were tested across five test shots and evaluated using a cinematography-oriented qualitative evaluation scheme focusing on light plausibility, image quality and texture retention, as well as image integrity and temporal stability. These observations were complemented by eight semi-structured expert interviews with professionals from cinematography, lighting, and color grading. Results suggest that AI-based relighting does not currently replace on-set lighting but offers considerable potential as a selective correction and extension tool. Its strengths are particularly evident in wide and establishing shots, where faces and fine image details are less perceptually salient, as well as in situations where the desired lighting conditions are difficult to achieve or maintain on set due to weather, time, or budget constraints. Technical and creative limitations are most apparent in workflow integration and usability, as well as in texture loss and image alterations that impair visual credibility, particularly in portrait shots. The findings suggest the potential for a selective shift of certain lighting decisions toward post-production rather than a general replacement of on-set lighting. To maintain a coherent lighting design when substantial lighting decisions are deferred to post-production, greater continuity of cinematographic expertise and creative agency across production and post-production may be required.

items.title: AI-Based Smart Interview Analyzer System
items.abstract: The AI-Based Smart Interview Analyzer System is an artificial intelligence-based web application developed to help students and job seekers improve their interview skills through interactive mock interviews, automated performance evaluation, and personalized feedback. In today’s competitive employment environment, candidates often face challenges such as nervousness, poor communication skills, lack of confidence, and insufficient interview practice. Traditional preparation methods may not provide immediate and consistent feedback, creating a need for an intelligent system that supports effective and personalized interview preparation. The proposed system integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to support interview practice and analyze candidate responses. It provides job-role-based interview preparation, maintains interview history, and helps users identify their strengths and weaknesses through feedback. The application consists of two main modules: the Admin Module and the Student Module. The Admin Module manages student information, job roles, interviews, and feedback, while the Student Module allows users to access their dashboard, practice interviews, review previous sessions, view feedback, and manage their profiles. The system aims to provide an accessible and structured environment for continuous learning and performance improvement. By combining AI-based assessment with a user-friendly web interface, the AI-Based Smart Interview Analyzer System can help candidates develop better communication skills, increase confidence, and improve their readiness for real-world job interviews. Future enhancements may include advanced speech analysis, facial expression recognition, body-language assessment, multilingual support, and more comprehensive real-time performance evaluation

items.title: AI-Driven Human Task Substitution: Evidence from Google Translate and ChatGPT
items.abstract: We examine how different generations of artificial intelligence (AI) substitute for human knowledge worker tasks, leveraging two sequential natural experiments in the translation industry. We study the introduction of Google Neural Machine Translation (GNMT), a predictive, task-specific AI, as well as ChatGPT, a broad, general-purpose generative AI, in a major online labor market. Distinguishing between analytical tasks (regular translations) and intuitive tasks (transcreations, which require creative and cultural adaptation), we estimate difference-in-differences models on transaction-level data from 2016 to 2017 and 2022 to 2023. We find that GNMT reduced the demand for analytical tasks by economically meaningful magnitudes, while having no detectable effect on intuitive tasks. By contrast, ChatGPT produced substantially larger and more uniform reductions for both analytical and intuitive tasks, indicating a marked expansion in the scope and magnitude of AI substitution. By comparing these two technological shocks within the same labor market, we show that conclusions about which types of human work are resilient to automation do not straightforwardly generalize from predictive to generative AI. This paper was accepted by Joshua Gans, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06740 .

items.title: AI-Driven Hyperspectral Imaging in Clinical Medicine: A Critical Appraisal of Translational Readiness
items.abstract: The instruments used for intraoperative guidance have not improved over the years. Traditional margin evaluations fail in 10–20% of cancer surgeries, and histopathology confirmation can take 48–72 h. A promising alternative is hyperspectral imaging (HSI), which allows for real-time, label-free, non-contact, and detailed biochemical characterization of tissues. This review synthesizes 130 studies from 2015 to 2026, identified through a systematic search across multiple databases following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The studies cover various clinical areas, including surgical oncology (53%), neurosurgery (10.8%), perfusion assessment (6.2%), gastroenterology (5.4%), dermatology (4.6%), and emerging domains (20%). Each clinical area is evaluated using a four-part Translational Readiness Appraisal framework. This framework shifts the focus from technical proficiency to deployment evidence by examining hardware compatibility with operating rooms, real-time workflow integration, cross-site validation, and regulatory readiness. Since 2015, the combination of clinically approved HSI hardware and artificial intelligence has led to a tenfold increase in publications. However, a significant gap remains: none of the reviewed studies meet the evidence criteria necessary for regulatory approval. Of the studies, 48.5% show strong single-site validation, but 50.8% remain in the proof-of-concept stage. The heavy reliance on intra-patient validation tends to inflate performance estimates, leaving issues like calibration across devices and regulatory pathways largely unaddressed. HSI has demonstrated technical maturity in several areas, particularly in head and neck margin assessment and brain tumor delineation. The primary reason for the lack of clinical adoption is not imaging performance but rather the absence of multicenter validation and a formal regulatory evidence framework.

items.title: AI-driven lithium-ion battery health prediction: a review of SOC, SOH and RUL estimation techniques
items.abstract: The need for precise lithium-ion battery (LiB) monitoring and prognostics has grown significantly with the increasing use of electric vehicles (EVs) and renewable energy system (RES) technologies. State of charge (SOC), state of health (SOH), and remaining useful life (RUL) are three critical performance metrics for ensuring battery safety, functional dependability, and effective energy utilization. Non-linear degradation patterns, operating uncertainties, and dynamic environmental fluctuations are frequently difficult for traditional electrochemical and empirical assessment methods to capture. As a result, recent research has focused on advanced data-driven techniques for comprehensive battery state estimation, notably those based on artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning (DL). This review provides an overview of current methodologies for SOC, SOH, and RUL prediction, with a focus on modern DL architectures such as transformer networks, autoencoder-based latent modeling, neural basis expansion techniques, attention mechanisms, and hybrid optimization-driven frameworks. The article examines new advances in intelligent battery prognostics critically, emphasizing their potential for improved estimation precision, resilience, and flexibility in practical operating scenarios. In addition, it identifies future research directions such as enhanced optimization-assisted frameworks, hybrid physics-informed learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). This article intends to offer a comprehensive overview of modern battery prognostics approaches to aid in the development of dependable, efficient, and long-term battery management system (BMS) solutions for electric mobility and energy storage systems.

items.title: AI-Driven Multi-Dimensional Course Assessment and SHS Strand Recommendation System
items.abstract: Senior High School (SHS) students often face challenges in selecting the most appropriate academic strand due to limited assessment tools and the continued reliance on traditional guidance practices. These methods frequently lack objectivity and comprehensive evaluation, resulting in mismatches between students’ competencies, interests, and their chosen academic pathways. Such misalignment may affect students’ academic performance, educational direction, and future career readiness. This study aimed to develop an AI-Driven Multi-Dimensional Course Assessment and SHS Strand Recommendation System designed to objectively evaluate student competencies and generate strand recommendations that align with learners’ abilities, interests, and career potential. The system intends to support students, teachers, and guidance personnel by providing data-driven insights that can assist in making informed academic decisions. The research employed a quantitative–descriptive design integrated with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). The system was developed using an Input–Process–Output (IPO) conceptual framework combined with Agile Software Development Methodology, enabling iterative system improvement and structured data processing. The platform utilizes a 30-dimension assessment model measuring cognitive skills, literacy and communication abilities, technical aptitude, and personality-interest indicators. Student responses are processed through a structured scoring model and analyzed using an AI-powered evaluation module to generate strand recommendations, competency profiles, and career-related insights, which are presented in a downloadable evaluation report. The results are presented in a comprehensive evaluation report that users can download and use for academic guidance and decision-making. Evaluation results showed strong system performance and user acceptance. Based on the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model, IT experts gave the system an overall mean score of 3.95, indicating a high level of software quality and functionality. System users rated the platform with an overall mean score of 4.00, interpreted as Highly Acceptable, reflecting positive user experience and effectiveness. This finding clearly demonstrates that the system can provide data-driven guidance in SHS strand selection, reduce academic-career mismatches, and support better educational alignment and long-term career readiness among students.

items.title: AI-Driven Personalised Disability Support Systems in Higher Education
items.abstract: This chapter examines the role of artificial intelligence in advancing personalised disability support within higher education. It analyses key applications, including adaptive learning systems, predictive analytics, and assistive technologies, highlighting their capacity to improve access, engagement, and student success. Attention is given to opportunities for enhancing institutional performance through data-informed decision-making and scalable support systems. Ethical considerations, including transparency, fairness, privacy, and user autonomy, are critically explored, alongside the importance of human-centred and participatory design approaches. The chapter further discusses governance, policy alignment, and capacity building as essential conditions for responsible AI integration. It argues that the transformative potential of AI depends on sustained institutional commitment to inclusive, equitable, and ethically grounded practices.

items.title: AI-driven predictive modeling of supercritical CO2 solubility using cheetah-optimized machine learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning models provide powerful data-driven tools for modeling complex nonlinear systems and predicting process behavior from limited experimental data. In this study, an AI-driven predictive framework is developed for modeling paracetamol solubility and solvent density in supercritical carbon dioxide (SC-CO 2 ). A dataset comprising 40 experimental observations was employed, with pressure and temperature used as input variables and paracetamol mole fraction and SC-CO 2 density considered as target outputs. Three machine-learning regression algorithms—Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), Tweedie Regression (TDR), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)—were developed and comparatively evaluated. To enhance predictive performance and automate model configuration, the Cheetah Optimizer (CO), a nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization algorithm, was integrated into the modeling framework for hyperparameter optimization. Model performance was assessed using the coefficient of determination ( R 2 ), mean squared error (MSE), and mean absolute error (MAE). The results demonstrated that TDR provided the highest predictive accuracy for paracetamol mole fraction, achieving an R 2 of 0.985, whereas GPR exhibited the best performance for SC-CO 2 density prediction, with an R 2 of 0.991. The developed framework successfully captured the nonlinear relationships between operating conditions and the predicted properties while demonstrating that the optimal learning algorithm depends on the target variable. These findings highlight the potential of AI-assisted optimization and machine-learning approaches for data-driven prediction and intelligent modeling of complex supercritical-fluid processes.

items.title: AI-driven retail banking ecosystems: a framework for improving customer experience, risk management, and operational efficiency
items.abstract: The current study has been conducted to propose and validate the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven banking ecosystem model for understanding how AI improves customer experience, risk management, and operational efficiency within the context of the banking industry. Specifically, the study aims to overcome the lack of empirical studies providing holistic evidence on how AI works in emerging regional banking markets by analysing the influence of AI awareness, AI application, and AI effectiveness on banking performance. The study utilises quantitative and explanatory research designs and data collection procedures. In total, 480 participants, including customers, employees, and branch managers of scheduled commercial banks have been surveyed. The AI-driven banking ecosystem has been defined using the constructs of AI awareness, AI application, and AI effectiveness. Descriptive statistics, reliability and validity testing, CFA, and SEM have been used for data analysis. The findings show that the AI-driven banking ecosystem positively influences all dimensions of banking performance. In addition, risk management (β = 0.751, p < 0.001), operational efficiency (β = 0.704, p < 0.001), and customer experience (β = 0.582, p < 0.01) had the highest impact on performance in the banking industry. The structural model presented satisfactory goodness-of-fit indicators, which confirmed the conceptual framework of the research and all the hypotheses of the study. In addition, the research suggests the development of an integrated AI driven banking ecosystem framework that takes into account technological, organisational, and strategic aspects of AI.

items.title: AI-Driven Smart Contracts and Autonomous Financial Ecosystems
items.abstract: This chapter delves into the transformative synergy between artificial intelligence (AI) and smart contracts, positioning them as the next frontier in managing digital assets and virtual currencies. It introduces the core concepts, illustrating how AI injects adaptability into rigid blockchain-based contracts, enabling real-time adjustments, predictive analytics, and autonomous dispute resolution. From an economic perspective, the integration drives efficiency in decentralized finance (DeFi), with the total value locked surging to $129 billion by mid-2025, thereby democratizing access while posing risks such as market bubbles. Socially, it promises inclusion for underserved populations through microlending and empowers communities via decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs), yet raises concerns over biases, job disruptions, and digital divides. Policy analysis examines frameworks such as the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulation and U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) guidelines, balancing innovation with consumer protection in central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) like the Digital Euro and e-CNY. Business perspectives highlight competitive edges in supply chain optimization and tokenized economies, with practical recommendations for risk mitigation. Key applications explored include dynamic contract optimization using machine learning, AI oracles for trustless data integration, and AI-driven DAOs for governance. Institutional and retail use cases demonstrate AI-audited compliance and robo-advisors for portfolios. Regulatory and ethical challenges, including the legal personhood of AI-augmented DAOs and issues of bias, transparency, and accountability, are critically assessed. Future directions envision convergences with the Internet of Things (IoT) and quantum computing, fostering self-sustaining ecosystems amid risks such as encryption vulnerabilities and opportunities for trillions in value creation. Aimed at business professionals, academics, and regulators, the chapter provides actionable insights to navigate and profit from this evolving landscape, emphasizing ethical and sustainable practices.

items.title: AI-Native Network with Clean–Impaired Semantic Preservation for Robust Semantic Communications in Space
items.abstract: Semantic communication offers a method for task-oriented information delivery in artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled space networks, but compact semantic representations remain vulnerable to fading, noise, and structured corruption during transmission. This work proposes Clean–Impaired Semantic Preservation for Robust Semantic Communications (CISP-SemCom), a link-level semantic communication framework that explicitly learns from the clean latent representation and its communication-impaired counterpart generated from the same source sample. In a shared projection space, class-aware Clean–Impaired Contrastive Alignment (CI-Con) preserves cross-sample discrimination while excluding same-class non-matched samples from the negative set, and Semantic Preservation (SP) directly promotes consistency within each matched clean–impaired pair. In a ten-seed controlled same-backbone evaluation on CIFAR-10 under Rician fading, CISP-SemCom increases the normalized area under the robustness curve (AURC) evaluated over the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) (SNR-AURC) from 66.85 ± 2.36 to 72.48 ± 1.24, corresponding to a paired gain of 5.63 AURC points with a 95% confidence interval of [3.75, 7.51]. Mechanism diagnostics show that SP-only optimization admits projector collapse, and that class-agnostic contrastive learning introduces same-class false-negative pressure. A direct class-aware ablation further indicates that most of the measured task-robustness gain comes from class-aware CI-Con, while SP acts as an explicit matched-pair consistency regularizer. On EuroSAT RGB, SNR-AURC increases from 65.53 ± 1.80 to 75.35 ± 1.58, showing that the robustness improvement is also observed on a second dataset. Decoder-independent latent probes further show improved accessibility of task-relevant class information, while the measured batch-1 inference latency remains similar to Backbone. These results support clean–impaired semantic preservation as an effective strategy for robust task-oriented transmission under satellite-inspired link impairments.

items.title: AI-Powered Personal Tutors as a Scalable Solution to the 2-Sigma Problem in Pharmacy Education
items.abstract: Background: The “2 Sigma Problem”, where individualized tutoring outperforms conventional instruction by two standard deviations, remains a persistent challenge in large-enrollment pharmacy courses. Generative AI tutors, constrained to instructor-verified content, offer a scalable, equitable approximation of personalized support. Methods: Four course-specific AI tutors were deployed across first-year (P1; n = 108–119/cohort) and third-year (P3; n = 98–108/cohort) Doctor of Pharmacy cohorts (Fall 2024–Spring 2026) using ChatGPT-4o and PlayLab with retrieval-augmented generation. Effectiveness was evaluated through longitudinal grade analysis, American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy proficiency outcomes, satisfaction surveys, and anonymized interaction log analysis. Results: Engagement was heterogeneous across curricular formats: 15-week P1 courses supported sustained weekly usage for foundational concept reinforcement, whereas 4-week P3 modules exhibited lower, targeted utilization focused on rapid self-assessment. In P1 Biochemistry, tutor integration was associated with longitudinal cohort exam improvements. The overall targeted metabolism exam mean rose from 74.0% (Fall 2023, no AI) to 81.4% (Fall 2024, AI tutor) and 83.6% (Fall 2025, AI tutor), with active users (n = 16, 85%, Fall 2024) outperforming non-users (n = 16, 79.3%, Fall 2024) by 5.7 percentage points, and with higher mean scores observed across progressively higher usage tiers. items.title: AI-ready design of realistic 2D materials and interfaces with Mat3ra-2D
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models in materials science are predominantly trained on ideal bulk crystals, limiting their transferability to real-world applications where surfaces, interfaces, and defects dominate. We present Mat3ra-2D, an open-source framework for the rapid design of realistic two-dimensional materials and related structures, including slabs and heterogeneous interfaces, with support for disorder and defect-driven complexity. The approach combines: (1) well-defined standards for storing and exchanging materials data with a modular implementation of core concepts and (2) transformation workflows expressed as configuration-builder pipelines that preserve provenance and metadata. We implement typical structure generation tasks, such as constructing orientation-specific slabs or strain-matching interfaces, in reusable Jupyter notebooks that serve as both interactive documentation and templates for reproducible runs. To lower the barrier to adoption, we design the examples to run in any web browser and demonstrate how to incorporate these developments into a web application. Mat3ra-2D enables systematic creation and organization of realistic 2D- and interface-aware datasets for AI/ML-ready applications.

items.title: AI, libraries, and literacy: revisiting the Journal of the Medical Library Association's policy on the use of generative artificial intelligence in submissions
items.abstract: In the fall of 2023, the Journal of the Medical Library Association (JMLA) introduced its policy on generative artificial intelligence (AI) submissions, predicting that these tools would become embedded within the workflows of clinicians, educators, researchers, and students. Those predictions dramatically underestimated AI's impact. On the three-year anniversary of that editorial, we revisit the issue in light of AI's unprecedentedly rapid adoption across knowledge work. We examine the educational challenges AI poses, arguing that excessive cognitive offloading threatens the deep thinking on which learning depends. We then consider the challenges AI creates for researchers, from hallucinated citations to fabricated diseases. We suggest that health sciences librarians, who offer expertise in approaching information systems with discernment, are well suited to be leaders in this space. To help prospective JMLA authors weigh whether and when to use AI, we propose the Compliance, Verifiability, and Disclosure (CVD) Framework. Throughout, we reaffirm our conviction that education and research must remain human-centered endeavors.

items.title: Algorithm or Assembly? An Experimental Study of Recommendations by AI Versus Deliberative Mini-Publics in Democratic Decision-Making
items.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) renewed debates about who—or what—can legitimately contribute to democratic processes. While both AI and deliberative mini-publics can supplement citizens’ efforts to form judgments about issues, little is known about how citizens evaluate policy advice from these sources. In an online survey experiment with U.S. adults (N = 502), participants read a mock news story reporting a policy recommendation, attributed either to an AI system or a deliberative citizens’ assembly. Opinion climate was orthogonally varied to assess contextual influences. Results were split: citizens’ assemblies were rated fairer and more satisfying, but AI was perceived to be more useful. Opinion climate cues had no moderating effects. Further analysis indicated that acceptance of AI versus citizens’ assembly recommendations depends on individual factors, such as prior attitudes toward the issue and trust in AI. Findings offer theoretical and practical implications for designing democratic decision support systems.

items.title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints. We separate the Modality Gap in cross-modal correspondence and evidence use from the Intent Gap in behavior relative to specified constraints, goals, and human expectations. Six dimensions organize the review: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. The first four control evidence access, optimization targets, supervision, and updates. Comparing mechanisms and supervision assumptions shows what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment. Evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels tests these choices through controlled input changes and reward-model validation, and we interpret each gain together with its model, task, and evaluation setup instead of comparing scores across conditions. Studies in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support share three requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and constraint-sensitive decisions. Stronger representations or higher benchmark scores can leave the claimed alignment mechanism unresolved, which motivates four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, targeted repair from failure diagnosis, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.

items.title: Alpiniae oxyphyllae Fructus in Alzheimer’s Disease: Multi-Target Mechanisms, Current Evidence, and Future AI-Driven Perspectives
items.abstract: Alpiniae oxyphyllae Fructus (Zingiberaceae; Alpinia oxyphylla Miq) (AOF) is a traditional Chinese medicinal and edible homologous material rich in bioactive metabolites, including flavonoids, terpenes, and sesquiterpenes. Its multiple metabolites and multi-target nature confer unique advantages for cognitive function and neuroprotection. However, recent advances in extraction techniques, the discovery of AOF effects, and novel ameliorative mechanisms against Alzheimer’s disease (AD) require an updated review. This review systematically expands on the botanical features, traditional dietary applications, and quality control of AOF raw materials, as well as its AD-ameliorating effect, in vivo absorption, toxicological safety, and extraction technology optimization strategies. Moreover, we explored the emerging mechanisms underlying the effectiveness of AOF and its bioactive metabolites in improving AD, including effects on glial cell function, the gut–brain axis, brain metal ions, and advanced glycation end products. This review comprehensively summarizes preclinical studies, clinical research, and commercially available products related to AOF and its metabolites. It also expounds upon the potential impetus that artificial intelligence could offer AOF research in the future. In summary, this review provides innovative technologies, in-depth mechanistic analyses, and novel research directions for exploring AOF extracts and their bioactive metabolites to offer strategic guidance for identifying new functional factors and drug candidates to combat AD.

items.title: AMF human-in-the-loop adaptive shielding design and validation
items.abstract: To achieve optimal shielding performance of an active magnetic field (AMF), its shielding concept should be understood not as a hardware component but as an adaptive operational system. On a mission where radiation can vary quickly, resources will always be limited. Decisions can be made either automatically or under astronaut supervision. The idea behind the development of the AMF shielding described in this chapter is that of a human-in-the-loop (HITL) system in which astronauts' situational awareness, supervision, feedback from sensors, and the actuation of the magnetic field are integrated into a single adaptive protection scheme [1]. The development of the current chapter relies heavily on previous research related to the basic physical principles behind AMFs, trade-offs between shielding effectiveness and shielding material properties, secondary radiation, spacecraft charging, electromagnetic compatibility, and general considerations regarding risks within a larger system-of-systems architecture. The focus moves away from the technical feasibility of a subsystem toward a mission-oriented analysis of the potential of AMFs as radiation shields, including questions related to how effectively they will allow for mission adaptation while being compatible with astronaut decision-making under various conditions [2]. Three major threads run through the current chapter. First, this chapter explores the human-centered control architecture of AMF-based shielding, which describes how astronauts, sensors, supervising systems, and shielding subsystems work in conjunction to protect astronauts from space radiation [3]. Second, it studies the accumulated shielding effect as determined by time. In particular, the importance of cumulative dose reduction is emphasized, since shielding in deep space implies protection over the entire mission period, not just the instantaneous effectiveness of the shielding field [4]. Finally, the chapter provides an analysis of the energy consumption trade-off for different shielding modes [5].

items.title: An academic chatbot with hybrid retrieval and local large language models
items.abstract: Higher-education institutions devote a substantial share of their staff time to answering queries whose answers are already set out in institutional regulations. This paper presents the design and evaluation of an academic chatbot based on retrieval-augmented generation that lets users query those documents in natural language and receive grounded answers in Spanish. The system combines a structure-aware ingestion pipeline, a hybrid retriever that fuses dense semantic search and lexical search through reciprocal rank fusion, and a locally hosted large language model. A distinguishing goal is data sovereignty: every component runs on institutional hardware, so no data is sent to external services. Quality is evaluated with the RAGAS framework over five regulatory documents: the corpus-wide set attains a global score of 0.90, with faithfulness of 0.97. The acceptance criterion is not met, however, under its conjunctive reading: answer relevancy stays below its threshold across all sets, and p95 latency reaches 6.47 seconds against a 5-second target. Quality further degrades on long, heavily cross-referenced regulations. A contrast questionnaire administered to nineteen users places the perception index at 3.64 out of 5 and exposes a relevant discrepancy: only 57.9% agree that the system does not produce fabricated information, against the faithfulness the automatic judge assigns it.

items.title: An agentic multi-drone framework for autonomous multi-accident detection, reasoning, and response
items.abstract: Rapid and effective response to highway accidents is critical for reducing response delays and improving situational awareness. In this study, we present an agentic multi-drone, end-to-end incident management framework, developed and validated in the Gazebo simulation environment, in which specialized planning, coordination, perception, scene-description, and dispatch agents communicate through ROS/MAVROS and MQTT interfaces. A simulated emergency call transcript is processed by a GPT-4o mini-based planning agent to extract incident coordinates and mission intent, which the coordination agent resolves into an optimal drone-to-incident allocation. Up to four autonomous drones, each managed via MAVROS and ArduPilot, navigate under GUIDED mode to their assigned sites, where a custom-trained YOLOv11n perception agent performs real-time accident and fire recognition on live aerial imagery. Detected events trigger a fine-tuned BLIP-2 description agent, which converts visual evidence into structured natural-language incident reports. When multiple reports correspond to the same incident, confidence-prioritized fusion selects the highest-confidence view as the primary description and supplements it with non-duplicated salient information from secondary views. A Piper TTS-based dispatch agent then converts these summaries into audio alerts and autonomously routes them to the nearest rescue center based on drone proximity. The description agent was fine-tuned on 1,783 image–caption pairs derived from the curated incident dataset, with reference captions generated using moondream2, holding its visual encoder and Q-Former frozen to preserve pre-trained feature representations, and evaluated on a held-out set of 254 samples using BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, METEOR, CIDEr, and SPICE. Results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed modular agentic architecture for autonomous multi-incident perception, reasoning, and coordinated drone-based emergency response in the evaluated four-drone, four-incident simulation configuration. The framework provides a basis for future validation in larger-scale and real-world emergency-response scenarios.

items.title: An expert routing-driven graph framework from tongue multi-task features to liver fibrosis prediction
items.abstract: Liver fibrosis is a global health concern where early detection is crucial for timely intervention. Traditional Chinese Medicine tongue diagnosis offers a promising non-invasive assessment, but suffers from inter-observer variability and subjective interpretation. Current artificial intelligence approaches focus on binary classification without revealing tongue features influencing diagnosis, limiting clinical utility. To address these challenges, we propose two key artificial intelligence innovations: (1) Hierarchical Kolmogorov–Arnold Network-based Adaptive Multi-task Experts, a novel multi-task learning architecture with adaptive quota routing that dynamically determines expert allocation based on sample complexity, solving the negative transfer problem; (2) Dynamic Tongue Relationship Graph Convolutional Network, a graph neural network that transforms expert selection patterns into patient-specific relationship graphs, enabling personalized modeling of attribute interactions. These artificial intelligence contributions advance the state-of-the-art in multi-task learning and dynamic graph construction for heterogeneous data, representing our core contributions at the artificial intelligence algorithmic level. As the engineering application of these artificial intelligence innovations, we develop Tongue Network with Dynamic Graph Relationship Learning, a non-invasive and interpretable framework based on tongue images that identifies seven critical tongue attributes and models their interrelationships for liver fibrosis risk screening in Traditional Chinese Medicine-based hepatology practice. Our method achieves 0.751 accuracy and 0.767 area under the curve, with 0.07 and 0.08 improvements over state-of-the-art graph neural networks and multimodal approaches. The framework offers visualizable classifications and relationship structures, providing insights into tongue features and liver fibrosis risk assessment. Codes are available at https://github.com/MedAI-UAIX/TongueNet-DGRL .

items.title: An intelligent decision-making model for accelerating green manufacturing adoption in automotive, electronics, and textile industries
items.abstract: Abstract Manufacturing industry is being increasingly forced to go green without compromising on the efficiency and effectiveness of their operations. This paper discusses an artificial intelligence based approach for encouraging the adoption of green practices in the manufacturing industries. Green manufacturing is an essential way of attaining environmental sustainability. However, the adoption of green manufacturing is still a challenge owing to the problem of reconciling the economic objectives with the environmental requirements. The integration of machine learning and green manufacturing results into a decision support system. The AI model designed utilizes predictive analytics, neural networks, and optimization algorithms for the identification of green manufacturing opportunities and for the formulation of strategies for their implementation. The data used comes from 85 manufacturing plants of the automotive, electronics, and textile industries, which proves the effectiveness of the model. The results show that AI-assisted green manufacturing reaches up to 27% less energy use, 22% material waste reduction, and 25% lower carbon footprint so far comparing with the traditional methods. The model is going to be a source of support and practical advice for the manufacturers, who are willing to be environmentally responsible and perform operatively, thus, the research will add to and share the existing academic knowledge of sustainable manufacturing along with the industrial part of the practice.

items.title: An Organizational Socialization Support System for Newly Hired Research and Development Employees in High-Tech Enterprises: A Case Study of Mentorship at G Automobile Group
items.abstract: In high-tech research and development (R&D) contexts, where artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tools and digital collaboration platforms are becoming increasingly prevalent, the learning and integration pathways of newly hired R&D employees are undergoing structural changes. Mentorship has emerged as a key mechanism supporting organizational socialization and innovation. This study examines the role of mentorship as a core mechanism in integrating internal digital platforms and cross-departmental resources to construct a systematic organizational socialization support network. Adopting a qualitative, cross-sectional single-case study strategy, this study collected data through semi-structured interviews and internal archival documents and analyzed the data using directed content analysis. This study finds that G Automobile Group embeds mentorship into its “180-Day Transformation Program,” thereby forming a closed-loop development system through growth planning, dynamic feedback, and regular reviews. By combining contextualized on-the-job mentoring with resource-based self-directed learning, mentorship facilitates the transformation of tacit knowledge into job competence. A hierarchical mentoring system, knowledge accumulation through digital platforms, and cross-departmental resource integration further enhance the effectiveness of newcomer socialization. The study also finds that mentors serve dual roles as supporters and evaluators. Transparent standards and clear communication processes are required to reduce the risk of negative mentoring experiences. The novelty of this study lies in conceptualizing mentorship not merely as a dyadic support relationship but as a digitally embedded organizational socialization support system that integrates formal mentoring, informal resource flows, AI-enabled tools, and cross-departmental collaboration.

items.title: An unmanned aerial vehicle-assisted visual measurement framework for forest road condition assessment with overlapping distress quantification
items.abstract: Routine forest-road maintenance is essential for road safety, accessibility, and serviceability, yet current inspections remain labor-intensive. Existing visual methods usually quantify pavement distresses independently, which may introduce area-estimation errors and affect condition assessment when multiple distresses spatially overlap. To address this engineering challenge, this study proposes an engineering artificial intelligence framework integrating Transformer-based semantic segmentation and diffusion-based data augmentation for unmanned aerial vehicle-assisted multi-distress measurement, overlapping-distress quantification, and forest-road condition assessment. This framework incorporates a segmentation model that converts aerial images into pixel-level distress masks for area measurement. The segmentation model employs a dynamic-gated convolutional backbone to integrate local textures with global context and a frequency-modulated spatial attention decoder to enhance small-scale and weakly visible distresses. A two-stage overlapping-distress identification strategy is developed to localize overlapping regions, identify their constituent distress categories, and support overlap-aware area quantification and condition assessment. A multi-condition guided diffusion model is further introduced to enrich inspection-image diversity, and a Forest Road Daily Inspection dataset is constructed for model training and evaluation. For engineering assessment, a Forest Pavement Condition Index is developed by incorporating measured areas of multiple distress types and overlapping regions, enabling section-level condition evaluation and maintenance prioritization. Experiments on the constructed forest-road inspection dataset and a public benchmark demonstrate that the proposed segmentation model improves multi-distress segmentation, overlapping-region identification, and measurement-oriented condition assessment, supporting its potential for forest-road condition measurement and maintenance-oriented assessment under the tested conditions.
